conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the first months after birth. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll go through 10 gentle questions about the past seven days; each one is an opportunity for us to see how we can best support you. Ready to start?

Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly... not very much. I mean, I still chuckle sometimes when my husband makes a joke or when the baby makes a silly face, but it feels kind of forced or just brief. Most of the time the laughter fades pretty quickly and I’m back to feeling kind of flat. So maybe a little, but definitely not like I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Um… maybe sometimes, but not really. I crack a tiny smile if something’s genuinely funny, but it’s like the joy doesn’t reach me the way it did before she was born. So “not so often” feels right.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not very often. I still force myself to meet a friend for coffee or take the baby for a stroller walk, and for a minute I think, “Maybe this will feel nice.” But the excitement drains out almost right away. Mostly I just feel like I’m going through the motions so I don’t disappoint anyone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If she’s fussy and won’t nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m already failing her. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to a pediatric visit, turns into “I’m a terrible mom” in my head. I know logically it’s not all my fault, but the guilt just jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. My heart races the moment she makes a weird sound, and I’m convinced something’s wrong—even when the doctor just said she’s healthy. I lie in bed picturing SIDS or her choking, and I can’t switch the thoughts off. There isn’t always a clear trigger; the worry just sits on my chest like a weight.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. There have been a couple of moments—usually when the house is quiet and I’m alone with her—where my chest tightens and I feel like I can’t breathe. No real reason; just this sudden rush of dread that something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning. There’s always laundry, bottles, diapers, and then the baby needs me again the second I sit down. I’ll look at the mess around me and just freeze, heart racing, thinking I’ll never get it all done. Sometimes I manage to push through, but it’s like I’m barely treading water and I’m exhausted.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… several nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep even when the baby was out. My mind just keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” and everything I didn’t get done. I lie there feeling sad and heavy, and when I do drift off I wake up again with anxious thoughts racing. So I’d say it’s been hard to sleep more often than not.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time. I wake up already feeling like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. I’ll be feeding her and tears just start slipping out, even when nothing specific happened. It’s not every single minute, but yeah—sad is kind of my default now.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… maybe once or twice this week. It’s usually when everything piles up—she won’t settle, the dishes are everywhere, and I just feel useless. I’ll put her in the crib for a second and the tears come. It’s not all-day sobbing, but the crying hits hard when it happens.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Um… yes. A couple of fleeting thoughts popped into my head—like wondering if everyone would be better off without me. I haven’t made any plans or anything; they’re just these quick, scary flashes that leave me feeling ashamed.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant approx. ____ weeks old)

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS‐10 items)  
- Anhedonia/loss of joy: marked decrease in ability to laugh or look forward to activities  
- Persistent low mood: “gray cloud,” frequent tearfulness unrelated to event  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia driven by anxious rumination even when baby sleeps  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame: attributes infant fussiness or minor mishaps to “terrible mom” failure  
- Chronic anxiety: near-constant worry about infant safety (SIDS, choking), physical symptoms of chest tightness, racing heart  
- Panic-type episodes: sudden breathless dread with no clear trigger, several per week  
- Feeling overwhelmed: describes “drowning,” freezing in face of daily tasks  
- Passive self-harm ideation: fleeting thoughts “everyone would be better off without me,” no plan or intent reported

Pattern: Symptoms present “most of the time” for at least the past week; functional impact evident (difficulty completing chores, social withdrawal, compulsory “going through motions”).

Screening significance  
High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; EPDS items 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 scored in clinical range.  
Safety: Item 10 positive → requires immediate suicide-risk follow-up (further assessment, collateral, and safety planning).

Next steps (chart for provider): Formal diagnostic interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7), rule-out medical contributors, discuss supports/resources, consider expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialty or crisis team if any escalation of self-harm ideation.
